newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu crossed threshold with Hebron, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu crossed threshold with Hebron, U.S. says.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "crossed an important threshold" by agreeing a Hebron deal and the move was bound to improve ties with the Arab world, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Friday.

In an interview with international news agencies, Christopher also said now was the time for Israel to "test the willingness" of Syria to resume peace talks, despite the apparent unwillingness of Damascus to do so.
Christopher stopped short of saying that Netanyahu had been converted to the "land-for-peace" principle under Wednesday's Hebron deal handing most of the West Bank town to the Palestinians.

But he said: "I think he's crossed an important threshold. He came into office vowing not to talk with (Palestinian) Chairman (Yasser) Arafat and he has now engaged in discussions with him and they've been able to reach this agreement."

Christopher, who leaves office next Monday, compared the development of Netanyahu's ties with Arafat to those of Israel's former Labour Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated in November, 1995 by a Jewish extremist.

Rabin and Arafat "had very distant relationships at the beginning but they began to find a basis of working together. So I think the Prime Minister (Netanyahu) has recognised the need for pragmatism," Christopher said.

"There's no doubt this will improve the relationships between Israel and the rest of the Arab world," which has been sceptical as to whether Netanyahu has been willing to proceed with past peace agreements with the Palestinians, he said.

"By reaching this agreement, by beginning redeployment ... by committing to a road map for the future, he will give, I think, some encouragement to those Arab countries that have wanted to see progress in peace."

Despite Syria's apparent lack of interest in resuming peace talks, which broke down almost a year ago over the issue of the Golan Heights seized by Israel in 1967, Christopher said it should not be assumed that no progress was possible.

"I would think that the Israeli government...should test the willingness of the Syrians to engage in serious discussions," said Christopher, who made some 20 trips to Damascus in his four-year tenure without reaching an accord.

Despite the Hebron accord, the official Syrian newspaper al-Thawra said on Friday there was nothing new to encourage Syria to resume peace talks with Israel. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Thursday he saw no sign that talks were likely to be revived in the near future.

Christopher said violent incidents like a bomb explosion -- blamed by Syria on Israeli agents -- that killed nine people on a bus in Damascus on Dec. 31 underscored the need for peace in the Middle East.
"I would think that any incidents within Syria might remind them of the importance of pursuing peace and creating a situation of greater tranquility and greater stability in the region," he said.

Christopher said he had no detailed knowledge of the health of Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, 66, who Syrian officials said underwent successful prostate surgery this month. "I'm told he will soon be back in action," he said.
